question: What does a typical mobile CI pipeline look like?
answer:
A mobile pipeline is really two pipelines — a fast lane that must finish while the reviewer is still looking at the PR, and a slow lane that may take an hour — and most of the design work is deciding what belongs in which.

Fast lane, on every PR:
• Lint and static analysis — Detekt and ktlint on Android, SwiftLint and SwiftFormat on iOS, `dart analyze` for Flutter.
• Unit tests on the JVM or a simulator. No emulator, no signing, no uploads.

Slow lane, on main or nightly:
• Instrumented and UI tests on an emulator or simulator.
• Release builds, signed with material pulled from secrets.
• Artifact upload to TestFlight or Play internal testing for QA.
• Symbol upload (dSYMs, ProGuard mapping) so crash reports de-obfuscate.
• Staged rollout, driven by fastlane lanes or the store APIs.

Providers: GitHub Actions is the common default, with Bitrise and Codemagic as mobile-specialised options, plus CircleCI, Buildkite, and Xcode Cloud for iOS-only shops.

Rules that keep it healthy:
• Keep the PR build under about fifteen minutes, or people stop reading the results.
• Cache Gradle, SwiftPM and CocoaPods deliberately; an uncached mobile build is mostly downloading.
• Run everything you can on Linux runners. macOS runners cost several times more per minute, so reserve them for work that genuinely requires Xcode.
• Signing material never lives in the repository. It comes from encrypted secrets, is decoded at build time, and is never echoed into a log.
code_example:
# .github/workflows/android.yml — the fast PR lane
name: Android CI
on:
  pull_request: { branches: [main] }
  push: { branches: [main] }
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v5
        with: { distribution: 'zulu', java-version: '17' }
      - uses: gradle/actions/setup-gradle@v6      # caches, and validates the wrapper
      - run: ./gradlew detekt lintDebug
      - run: ./gradlew testDebugUnitTest
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v6
        if: failure()
        with: { name: test-reports, path: '**/build/reports/' }

  instrumented:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest      # KVM on Linux is faster AND far cheaper than a macOS runner
    needs: test
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - name: Enable KVM
        run: |
          echo 'KERNEL=="kvm", GROUP="kvm", MODE="0666", OPTIONS+="static_node=kvm"' \
            | sudo tee /etc/udev/rules.d/99-kvm4all.rules
          sudo udevadm control --reload-rules && sudo udevadm trigger --name-match=kvm
      - uses: reactivecircus/android-emulator-runner@v2
        with:
          api-level: 36
          script: ./gradlew connectedDebugAndroidTest

# .github/workflows/ios.yml — macOS runners only where Xcode is unavoidable
# jobs:
#   test:
#     runs-on: macos-latest
#     steps:
#       - uses: actions/checkout@v6
#       - run: bundle exec fastlane scan --device "iPhone 17"

question: What is Fastlane and what does it automate?
answer:
Fastlane is a Ruby toolkit that turns the release ritual — build, sign, upload symbols, ship to a test track — into named lanes you run identically on a laptop and in CI.

Common automations:
• Build and sign — `build_app` (formerly `gym`) on iOS, the `gradle` action on Android.
• Code signing — `match` synchronises iOS certificates and provisioning profiles through a private, encrypted git repository (or S3, or Google Cloud Storage).
• Store authentication — `app_store_connect_api_key` loads an App Store Connect API key from an issuer id, key id and private key file. This is what CI should use; an Apple ID with an app-specific password is the legacy path and breaks on 2FA challenges.
• Beta distribution — `upload_to_testflight`, `firebase_app_distribution`, `upload_to_play_store` on the internal track.
• Production — `deliver` for the App Store, `supply` for Play, both scriptable including staged rollout percentages.
• Screenshots — `snapshot` drives UI tests across locales and devices, `frameit` decorates them, `deliver` uploads them.
• Symbols — `upload_symbols_to_crashlytics` and the Sentry plugin, so release crash reports are readable.

Why it survives: the same lane runs on a laptop and on CI, so 'works on my machine' becomes a testable claim. The alternative is a pile of bash that only one person understands, and that person is on holiday during the release.
code_example:
# fastlane/Fastfile — Android
default_platform(:android)

platform :android do
  desc "Build and upload to Play internal testing"
  lane :internal do
    gradle(task: "clean bundleRelease")
    upload_to_play_store(
      track: "internal",
      release_status: "draft",
      aab: "app/build/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab",
      mapping_paths: ["app/build/outputs/mapping/release/mapping.txt"]
    )
  end
end

# fastlane/Fastfile — iOS
platform :ios do
  desc "Build and upload to TestFlight"
  lane :beta do
    setup_ci if is_ci                      # keychain the runner can actually use

    # API key, not an Apple ID: unattended, and immune to 2FA prompts
    api_key = app_store_connect_api_key(
      key_id: ENV["ASC_KEY_ID"],
      issuer_id: ENV["ASC_ISSUER_ID"],
      key_content: ENV["ASC_KEY_P8"]
    )

    match(type: "appstore", readonly: is_ci, api_key: api_key)
    increment_build_number(xcodeproj: "MyApp.xcodeproj")
    build_app(scheme: "MyApp", export_method: "app-store-connect")
    upload_to_testflight(api_key: api_key, skip_waiting_for_build_processing: true)
    upload_symbols_to_crashlytics(gsp_path: "./MyApp/GoogleService-Info.plist")
  end
end

# In CI
# bundle exec fastlane android internal
# bundle exec fastlane ios beta

question: What does iOS code signing actually consist of, and how does CI get the certificates and profiles?
answer:
iOS signing is four moving parts that all have to agree: a certificate identifying who built the binary, a provisioning profile binding an App ID to that certificate, entitlements compiled into the app, and a bundle identifier that already exists in App Store Connect.

Getting the material onto CI:
• `fastlane match` stores certificates and profiles in a private repository, encrypted with a passphrase. CI clones and installs them in read-only mode, so a runner can never regenerate and thereby revoke the whole team's certificates.
• Authenticate with an App Store Connect API key rather than an Apple ID — two-factor authentication makes password auth unusable unattended.
• Xcode Cloud, or Xcode's automatic signing, is a reasonable choice for a small team that does not need the pipeline reproducible anywhere else.

Distribution paths:
• TestFlight — up to 100 internal testers with no review, up to 10 000 external testers behind a lighter review.
• App Store — full review, then either an immediate release or a phased rollout.
• Ad hoc and enterprise in-house distribution still exist but are narrow and increasingly legacy.

Gotchas that actually bite:
• Regenerating a profile can silently drop capabilities such as push or App Groups, and entitlements in the binary must match the profile exactly. That mismatch is caught at upload processing, not at build time, so it fails after the slow part.
• Apple raises the minimum build SDK every year; the current cycle requires uploads built with Xcode 26 and the iOS 26 SDK. Check the deadline before planning a release freeze, and do not confuse the build SDK with your deployment target.
• An expired certificate does not break installed apps, only new builds — so the failure always turns up on a deadline.
code_example:
# One-time setup, run by a human on a Mac
fastlane match init
fastlane match appstore              # creates or fetches cert + profile, encrypted into the repo

# CI: read-only, so a runner can never revoke the team's certificates
export MATCH_PASSWORD="${MATCH_PASSWORD}"
bundle exec fastlane match appstore --readonly

# Archive and export with explicit signing
xcodebuild -workspace MyApp.xcworkspace -scheme MyApp \
  -configuration Release -archivePath build/MyApp.xcarchive archive \
  CODE_SIGN_STYLE=Manual \
  PROVISIONING_PROFILE_SPECIFIER="match AppStore com.example.app" \
  CODE_SIGN_IDENTITY="Apple Distribution"

xcodebuild -exportArchive \
  -archivePath build/MyApp.xcarchive \
  -exportPath build \
  -exportOptionsPlist ExportOptions.plist

# Upload with an API key — no Apple ID, no 2FA prompt on a headless runner
bundle exec fastlane pilot upload --ipa build/MyApp.ipa

# ExportOptions.plist
# <key>method</key><string>app-store-connect</string>   <- 'app-store' is the old spelling
# <key>signingStyle</key><string>manual</string>
# <key>uploadSymbols</key><true/>

# Matchfile — note there is no username; auth comes from the API key
# git_url("git@github.com:org/certs.git")
# storage_mode("git")
# type("appstore")
# app_identifier(["com.example.app"])

# fastlane match nuke appstore    # revokes everything. Never from CI.

question: How do you sign and ship an Android app?
answer:
Android has two signing keys and the important one is not yours: you sign with an upload key, and Play App Signing re-signs the artifact with the app signing key that devices actually verify.

• Upload key — signs the AAB you upload. If you lose it, Play can reset it, which is the entire reason Play App Signing is worth using.
• App signing key — held by Google, used to sign the APKs delivered to devices.
• Build types: `debug` uses the shared debug keystore, `release` uses your keystore injected from CI secrets.
• The AAB is the required upload format. Play splits it per device by ABI, density and language, so what installs is never quite what you built — use `bundletool` when you need to reproduce a device's actual APK locally.

Distribution tracks:
• Internal testing — up to 100 testers, no review wait. This is where CI should push on every main-branch build.
• Closed and open testing — larger audiences, still reviewed.
• Production, with a staged rollout percentage you control and can halt.

Policy gates that block a release:
• Target API level, which Play raises annually. From 31 August 2026, new apps and updates must target Android 16 (API level 36), while existing apps need at least API level 35 to stay available to new users.
• A completed Data safety form and a privacy policy.
• 64-bit native libraries.
• An in-app account deletion path for apps with sign-in.

Keystore handling: base64 it into a CI secret, decode into the workspace at build time, delete it afterwards, and never echo the passwords into the log. Gradle will happily print them if you interpolate them into a task name.

question: What are build flavors / variants and when do you use them?
answer:
Flavors let you produce multiple APKs/AABs from one codebase, differing in package name, branding, endpoints, or features.

Android (Gradle):
• `productFlavors { free { ... }; paid { ... } }`
• Combined with `buildTypes { debug; release }` to give variants like `freeDebug`, `paidRelease`.
• Each flavor can override resources, manifests, source sets.

iOS (Xcode):
• Multiple targets — separate builds, separate Info.plist.
• Or schemes + xcconfig files — single target, different config files for dev / staging / prod.
• Asset catalogues + Info.plist substitution for branding.

Flutter:
• `--flavor` flag with `--dart-define` for compile-time constants.

Use flavors for:
• Dev / staging / prod with different API endpoints.
• White-label apps (same codebase, multiple branded apps).
• Free vs paid SKUs.
• Feature subsets per geography.

Keep flavor count small; each one multiplies your CI build matrix.

question: How do you do a staged rollout and observe a release?
answer:
Staged rollout = release to a small percent first, watch metrics, ramp.

Android (Play Console):
• Production → Releases → set rollout percentage (1%, 5%, 20%, 50%, 100%).
• Halt rollout if vitals drop. Resume when fixed (the affected version stays at the lower %).
• Internal app sharing — quick QA URLs.

iOS (App Store):
• Phased release for automatic updates: 1%, 2%, 5%, 10%, 20%, 50%, 100% over 7 days.
• Manual users get the app immediately.
• Pause / resume at any stage.
• Expedited review for critical fixes (use sparingly).

Observability during rollout:
• Crash-free users — Crashlytics / Sentry.
• ANR rate (Android) — Play Vitals.
• Frame rate / startup — Firebase Performance / MetricKit.
• Funnel + business metrics — Mixpanel / Amplitude.
• Server logs — error rate, latency.

Playbook: define KPIs and thresholds BEFORE shipping. Wire alerts (PagerDuty / Slack). Have a rollback plan: feature flags first, app pull-from-store as last resort.
code_example:
# fastlane — staged Play rollout
lane :production_5pct do
  upload_to_play_store(
    track: "production",
    rollout: "0.05",                 # 5%
    aab: "app/build/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab"
  )
end

lane :production_50pct do
  upload_to_play_store(
    track: "production",
    rollout: "0.5",
    skip_upload_apk: true,            # already uploaded
    skip_upload_aab: true
  )
end

# Halting via Play Console UI is recommended — fastlane can change rollout but the UI is faster in incidents.

# iOS phased release — toggle in App Store Connect:
# 'Phased Release for Automatic Updates' = ON

# Observability dashboard — track these on a per-version basis:
# - crash-free users (target > 99.5%)
# - ANR rate (target < 0.5%)
# - p99 cold startup (target < 2s)
# - business KPI: signup conversion, checkout success rate

# Rollback decision tree
# 1. Crash spike from new code path -> flip feature flag OFF
# 2. Cannot mitigate via flag -> halt rollout, ship hotfix in next update
# 3. Severe regression -> Play 'halt rollout' / iOS 'pause phased release', expedited review
